children: By Staff Writer

Kenyan large banks are set to bear heavier regulatory burden following a Central Bank of Kenya decision to regulate lenders depending on their size, which could stifle growth and dividend payout plans.

The CBK has issued guidelines putting more scrutiny on lenders classified as Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D-SIBs), given the disruption their collapse or distress would create in the local economy and regional market.

The regulations have placed a higher capital requirement threshold for the large banks, compared to the rest of the industry, while also requiring them to pay more licensing fees, which will be pegged on their revenues.

The regulator will look at the size of a lender, its interconnectedness with other institutions, complexity and substitutability (difficulty in being replaced in a specific service) – to determine if it will be classified as a domestic systemically important bank.

Previously, the large banks, including regional giants KCB Group, Equity Holdings, Cooperative Bank, NCBA Group and I&M Group, had enjoyed the same regulatory rigour as their smaller peers.“CBK may impose a surcharge on designated D-SIBs, implemented as an extension of the Capital Conservation Buffer known as Higher Loss Absorbency (HLA),” the regulator said.
HLA is implemented as a capital “add-on" or an extension to the existing CCB.“This supplementary buffer must be met exclusively using Common Equity Tier 1 capital,” it added.
Tier 1 capital is made up of ordinary shares and retained earnings, and serves as a cushion against financial stability.
The surcharge on the large banks will range from 0.5 percent to 2.5 percent of their risk weighted assets.

This means that the minimum ratio of core capital to total risk weighted assets for large banks can rise up to 15.5 percent up from the current 10.5 percent. The Central Bank has further introduced caps to the amount of profits that a bank can distribute as dividends capping it to its capital adequacy.
A bank may also be individually required to hold higher capital levels if the regulator deems it fit based on the stability of its business.

The large banks will also pay higher annual licence fees after CBK pegged the mandatory payments to a lender’s gross revenue. Commercial banks will pay to the regulator 0.13 percent of their gross revenues next year, which will grow to 0.14 percent in 2028 before settling at 0.15 percent.

CBK cited the growth of banks in size and regional expansion while increasing the licensing fees, stating it needed more resources to play its oversight responsibilities.“The annual fees payable under section 5(4) of the Act by an institution shall be at the rate of the gross annual revenue,” reads the Banking Fees Regulations of 2026.“The regulatory framework will impose additional financial costs on institutions licensed by CBK,” the regulator said in an impact assessment note on the new regulations.

Gross annual revenue includes income from interest on loans, advances, government securities, fees and commissions on loans and advances, dividend income, foreign exchange trading income, and any other income.

Currently, the industry uses a branch-based methodology with banks paying between Ksh30,000 ($231.57) and Ksh150,000 ($1,157.85) for each branch, depending on locations. They also pay head office charges of Ksh400,000 (3,087.61).

The Central Bank collected Ksh335 million ($2.59 million) under licence fees for the year ended June 2024, which the Bank estimates will grow to over Ksh950 million ($7.33 million) in the first year of implementing the new licence fees.

An impact assessment conducted by the regulator indicates that bank profits may decline 0.4 percent due to the new licence fees. This does not factor in the impact of other regulatory changes on a bank's performance.

The central bank has sought to have powers to restrict the introduction of products and expansion by banks deemed to be important financial institutions.“The supervisory measures deployed on a domestic systemically important financial institution depends on the supervisor's judgement as to the institution's degree of systemic risk,” states CBK in the draft regulation.

Kenyan banks have been eyeing new markets in Africa while deepening their presence in East Africa so as to grow revenues from regional operations. These plans will now have to be approved by the CBK based on analysis of the strength of a bank.
Equity Group Holdings, KCB Group, NCBA Group and Family Bank have declared intentions to spread their operations in new markets mainly in Southern Africa.
Equity Group said it is looking at Angola, Mozambique, Zambia, Ethiopia and Libya, as it targets to be in 15 countries in the next four years.
KCB, Kenya’s largest bank by asset base, is targeting to enter the Ethiopian market before the end of the year, indicating it had already identified prospective acquisition targets.
The new regulatory regime on the large banks is set to force them to review their dividend payouts, which have been generous in recent years.

Twelve listed banks paid total dividends of Ksh117.2 billion ($904.67 million) for the year ended December 2025, amounting to nearly half of the Ksh245.9 billion ($1.9 billion) that all Nairobi Securities Exchange-listed firms paid in their latest financial years.

For the full year ended December 2025, Co-operative Bank raised its dividend per share by 66.6 percent to Ksh2.50 ($0.019) from Ksh1.50 ($0.012) the previous year while Equity Group lifted its distribution by 35.2 percent to Ksh5.75 (0.044) per share.

title: ZAWYA: Banks growth could be eroded as Central Bank of Kenya imposes new licensing plan
